title: Congress Can Do More to Curb Kushner’s Conflicts of Interest
gist: Sarah Leah Whitson argues Jared Kushner's Gulf-funded Affinity Partners, now the top shareholder in Israeli conglomerate Phoenix Financial, creates sweeping conflicts while he negotiates for Trump, and that Congress left known ethics and FARA loopholes open. With Republicans controlling Congress, she sees only oversight pressure (special-government-employee status, recusal questions) as feasible now.

insights.claim: Affinity Partners, Kushner's investment firm, was financed overwhelmingly by Saudi Arabia and other Gulf monarchies, with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund putting in $2 billion shortly after launch.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: Gulf sovereign capital is the funding base of a firm run by a sitting US envoy; watch Gulf-linked flows and deal announcements involving Affinity.

insights.claim: At least 99 percent of Affinity's then-$3 billion under management came from foreign sources as of March 2024, principally Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which paid tens of millions annually in advisory fees.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: Near-total foreign-sovereign dependence ties the firm economics to Gulf government goodwill.
insights.locator: As a result of these investigations

insights.claim: CNN reported that Affinity Partners became the largest shareholder in Israeli conglomerate Phoenix Financial, which holds stakes in at least nine Israeli military suppliers, while Kushner was helping negotiate an Israel-Hamas peace deal.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: Israeli defense-supplier exposure via Gulf-sourced money is a live headline and reputational risk for all parties.

insights.claim: Kushner's first-term push for large weapons sales to Saudi Arabia and the UAE and his rehabilitation of Mohammed bin Salman after the Khashoggi murder are read by critics as repaid by the later Saudi investment in Affinity.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: If favors-for-capital is the model, expect Gulf investment to track US diplomatic outcomes favorable to Gulf states.

insights.claim: The same person managing billions for foreign governments is again shaping US policy toward them, including helping broker a potential multibillion-dollar sale of Russian oil assets to investors tied to his family and Steve Witkoff's.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: Russian oil-asset deal flow may be steered by envoys with personal financial links; watch for related transactions and sanctions relief.
insights.locator: But the problem for Americans is broader

insights.claim: Federal law did not bar Kushner from doing business with foreign governments after leaving office, private funds enjoy sweeping disclosure exemptions, and 'investment advisory services' payments from foreign governments avoid FARA disclosure.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: Structural loopholes mean similar revolving-door arrangements are legally repeatable by other ex-officials.

insights.claim: Congress gathered information through the Maloney (2022) and Wyden (2024) probes but passed no revolving-door law or FARA amendment, so Kushner's current activity went unconstrained.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: Absent legislation, the arrangement persists; legislative change is a low-probability catalyst.

insights.claim: There is essentially no prospect of meaningful reform in the next two years because Republicans control Congress and Democrats lack the subpoena power to test Kushner's claims.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: Expect no regulatory constraint on envoy conflicts before the next Congress; the risk is persistent rather than resolved.

insights.claim: Because even unpaid appointees can be special government employees subject to the conflict-of-interest recusal statute, Kushner arguably should be recused from Israel-Palestine, Russia-Ukraine, Saudi and UAE matters, but the administration has not designated him as one.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: A forced SGE designation or recusal would remove Kushner from key negotiations, a headline risk for the Gaza and Ukraine tracks.
insights.locator: Thankfully, Congress can still take steps

insights.claim: Whitson proposes a cooling-off period barring senior officials from doing business with foreign governments, disclosure of foreign-government investments in ex-officials' businesses, and closing the FARA investment-adviser loophole.
insights.speaker: Sarah Leah Whitson
insights.so_what: These are the reform items to watch if political control shifts.
insights.locator: Congress should also finally close the loopholes
